stimulus.text: "That whereas your poor and humble petitioner being condemned to die do humbly beg of you to take it into your judicious and pious considerations.... I petition to your honours not for my own life for I know I must die and my appointed time is set but the Lord he knows it is that if it be possible no more innocent blood may be shed." — Mary Easty, petition from Salem jail, September 1692 (abridged; spelling modernized).
stimulus.source_note: Mary Easty, petition to Governor Phipps and the Salem court, September 1692; public domain.

stem: The Puritan worldview that made witchcraft a plausible threat centered on

options.text: Deist belief in a distant clockmaker God who never intervenes.
options.misconception: Deism — a distant clockmaker God — belongs to Enlightenment figures like Franklin, not to Puritans.

options.text: Catholic devotion to the saints, the Virgin, and sacred relics.
options.misconception: Catholic devotion to the saints was exactly what Puritans rejected; their worldview was Reformed Protestant.

options.text: a cosmic struggle between God and Satan active in daily life.
Enlightenment rationalism and its cool trust in human reason alone.
options.misconception: Enlightenment rationalism was the opposite of the Puritan worldview: reason displacing the active supernatural.

rationales.general:
1. Ask what Puritans believed about the world. God and Satan were not distant ideas; both acted daily.
2. Ask what that makes of witchcraft. If Satan's agents work daily mischief, a witch is a real and present danger.
3. Rule out the later worldviews. Deism, Catholic sainthood, and Enlightenment reason belong to other minds.
4. Name the center. A cosmic war, fought in ordinary life, in which every soul had a side.
Remember: to a Puritan, witchcraft was not superstition — it was the enemy's daily work in a world at war.
rationales.C: Puritans lived inside an active cosmic war: God and Satan contended daily, and Satan's agents worked real mischief in ordinary life. Background: sickness, bad harvests, and strange fits were read as that mischief. Inside that worldview, witchcraft was a rational fear, not a superstition. Background: Easty's petition shows the human cost — a woman pleading that no more innocent blood be shed in a hunt driven by that fear. Deism, Catholic devotion, and Enlightenment rationalism all belong to other worldviews.
rationales.A: Deism — a distant clockmaker God — belongs to Enlightenment figures like Franklin, not to Puritans.
rationales.B: Catholic devotion to the saints was exactly what Puritans rejected; their worldview was Reformed Protestant.
rationales.D: Enlightenment rationalism was the opposite of the Puritan worldview: reason displacing the active supernatural.
